```{python}
#| include: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Arc
from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 13,
    "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.alpha": 0.25,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "legend.frameon": False,
})


def gaussian_pdf(x, mean, sigma):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mean) / sigma) ** 2) / (np.sqrt(2.0 * np.pi) * sigma)


def covariance_ellipse(mean, cov, k=1.0, n_points=200):
    """Points on the k-sigma ellipse of a 2D Gaussian, as a 2 x n_points array."""
    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov)
    angle = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0 * np.pi, n_points)
    circle = np.vstack([np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)])
    return mean[:, None] + k * eigenvectors @ np.diag(np.sqrt(eigenvalues)) @ circle
```

# Coordinate Frames and Attitude {#frames}

A number without a frame is a rumor.

[Chapter: Coordinate Frames and Attitude](https://jbrodovsky.github.io/advanced_navigation/chapters/01-foundations/frames-and-attitude.html)

## Same numbers, different worlds

[What does $[3,\ 4,\ -1]^T$ mean?]{.question}

. . .

Nothing yet. Say which frame.

::: {.incremental}
- In NED: 3 m north, 4 m east, 1 m **up**
- In ENU: 3 m east, 4 m north, 1 m **down**
- Positions, velocities, and quaternions can all look perfectly reasonable while
  describing different worlds
:::

::: {.notes}
Chapter opening. This chapter fixes the conventions before the IMU, camera,
GNSS, and filter chapters make the same choices less visibly. Ask the room who
has lost an afternoon to a sign or a frame. Everybody has.
:::

## The convention contract {auto-animate=true}

::: {data-id="contract"}
$$
\mathbf{v}^{\color{#1d4ed8}{a}} = \mathbf{C}_{\color{#b45309}{b}}^{\color{#1d4ed8}{a}}\,\mathbf{v}^{\color{#b45309}{b}}
$$
:::

::: {.incremental}
- [Superscript]{style="color:#1d4ed8; font-weight:600"}: the frame the
  coordinates are **written in**
- [Subscript]{style="color:#b45309; font-weight:600"}: the frame they **came
  from**
- Read right to left: a $b$-vector goes in, an $a$-vector comes out. The
  subscript of $\mathbf{C}$ must match the superscript it meets.
:::

::: {.notes}
The Convention Contract section. Spend time here: every later equation in the
course is written in this notation. C for a rotation (direction-cosine) matrix,
always; R is measurement noise.
:::

## The convention contract {auto-animate=true}

::: {data-id="contract"}
$$
\mathbf{v}^{\color{#1d4ed8}{a}} = \mathbf{C}_{\color{#b45309}{b}}^{\color{#1d4ed8}{a}}\,\mathbf{v}^{\color{#b45309}{b}}
$$
:::

The inverse is the transpose (proper rotations):
$\;\mathbf{C}_a^b = (\mathbf{C}_b^a)^T$

. . .

Chains compose when the inner indices match:

$$
\mathbf{C}_c^a = \mathbf{C}_b^a\,\mathbf{C}_c^b
\qquad
\mathbf{q}_c^a = \mathbf{q}_b^a \otimes \mathbf{q}_c^b
$$

. . .

::: {.key}
Body-to-navigation, $\mathbf{C}_b^n$, unless written otherwise. Never switch
silently between active and passive language: name both frames, then **test the
transform with a known vector**.
:::

## Book-wide conventions

::: {.smaller-text}
| | Convention |
|---|---|
| Navigation frame $n$ | North-east-down (NED) |
| Body frame $b$ | Forward-right-down (FRD); Project 1's drone body is $z$-up |
| Camera frame $c$ | Optical: $x$ right, $y$ down, $z$ along the optical axis |
| Angular rate | $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ab}^c$: frame $b$ relative to $a$, resolved in $c$ |
| Quaternions | Hamilton, scalar first $[q_w, q_x, q_y, q_z]^T$, with $\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}_b^n) = \mathbf{C}_b^n$ |
| Euler angles | Z-Y-X (yaw, pitch, roll), for display and initialization only |
| Errors | True minus estimate, $\delta\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}$; attitude errors are small rotations in $n$ |
| Rotation matrix | Always $\mathbf{C}$, never $\mathbf{R}$: $\mathbf{R}$ is measurement noise |
:::

. . .

When a dataset or library differs, convert **at the boundary** and say so in a
comment. The one deliberate exception: Project 1 uses its dataset's Z-X-Y Euler
sequence.

::: {.notes}
Book-Wide Conventions section. This is a reference slide; it appears at once.
Point out the Earth model letters too: this book follows Farrell (R_M meridian,
R_N prime vertical), and Groves uses different letters for the same radii.
Check a reference's convention before copying an equation from it.
:::

## NED is not ENU with new labels

```{python}
#| include: false
def arrow(ax, tip, label, offset, color="k"):
    ax.annotate("", xy=tip, xytext=(0.0, 0.0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=2.0, mutation_scale=18))
    ax.text(tip[0] + offset[0], tip[1] + offset[1], label, ha="center", va="center")


def vertical_axis(ax, out_of_page, label):
    ax.plot(0, 0, marker="o", ms=18, mfc="white", mec="k", mew=1.5, zorder=4)
    ax.plot(0, 0, marker="." if out_of_page else "x", ms=11 if out_of_page else 10,
            color="k", mew=2, zorder=5)
    ax.text(0.0, -0.32, label, ha="center", va="center")
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
$$
\mathbf{C}_{\text{NED}}^{\text{ENU}} =
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.incremental}
- Horizontal axes swap, the vertical flips
- A half turn about the north-east bisector: its own inverse
- Bodies too: FRD to FLU is $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1)$
- Yaw: $\psi_{\text{ENU}} = \pi/2 - \psi_{\text{NED}}$
:::
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}

## Euler angles are for display

$$
\mathbf{C}_b^n = \mathbf{R}_z(\psi)\,\mathbf{R}_y(\theta)\,\mathbf{R}_x(\phi)
$$

Roll $\phi$, pitch $\theta$, yaw $\psi$; in SciPy, `Rotation.from_euler("ZYX", [yaw, pitch, roll])`.

. . .

Reading them back:
$\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(C_{32}, C_{33})$,
$\;\theta = -\arcsin C_{31}$,
$\;\psi = \operatorname{atan2}(C_{21}, C_{11})$

. . .

At $\theta = \pm 90^\circ$ roll and yaw turn the body about the same axis, and
the extraction divides zero by zero: **gimbal lock**.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
a = Rotation.from_euler("ZYX", [30, 90, 10], degrees=True)   # yaw, pitch, roll
b = Rotation.from_euler("ZYX", [50, 90, 30], degrees=True)
print("same attitude:", np.allclose(a.as_matrix(), b.as_matrix()))
```

::: {.notes}
Rotation Matrices and Euler Angles section. Every sequence has a singularity
where its middle rotation reaches 90 degrees: pitch for Z-Y-X, roll for Project
1's Z-X-Y. At pitch +90 only yaw minus roll matters, so the two triples above
are one attitude. Hence Euler angles for display, plotting, and initialization,
never as internal states. Heading is not automatically yaw either (later slide).
:::

## Rotation vectors and the exponential map

Euler's rotation theorem: any rotation is one turn by $\theta$ about a unit axis
$\mathbf{u}$. Pack both into $\boldsymbol{\theta} = \theta\mathbf{u}$.

::: {.incremental}
- Three parameters, no singularity near the identity
- Exactly where navigation works: a gyro increment, an attitude error, a filter
  correction
:::

. . .

$$
\mathbf{C} = \exp\!\left([\boldsymbol{\theta}]_\times\right)
= \mathbf{I} + \sin\theta\,[\mathbf{u}]_\times + (1 - \cos\theta)\,[\mathbf{u}]_\times^2
$$

. . .

The series closes because $[\mathbf{u}]_\times^3 = -[\mathbf{u}]_\times$: odd
powers collect into $\sin\theta$, even powers into $1 - \cos\theta$.

. . .

Quaternion: $\mathbf{q} = [\cos(\theta/2),\ \mathbf{u}^T\sin(\theta/2)]^T$. The
**half angle** is why $\mathbf{q}$ and $-\mathbf{q}$ are the same attitude.

::: {.notes}
Rotation Vectors and the Exponential Map section (Rodrigues' formula). The
derivation uses [u]x^2 = u u^T - I for a unit vector. The axis is fixed by the
rotation (Cu = u), so it has the same coordinates in both frames. The inverse
map (the logarithm) goes through tr C = 1 + 2 cos(theta) and is ill-conditioned
near theta = pi; libraries switch methods there.
:::

## Quaternions in software

Hamilton and scalar first, $\mathbf{q} = [q_w, q_x, q_y, q_z]^T$. SciPy is
Hamilton too, but stores `[x, y, z, w]`.

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1-4|6-7|9-10|1-10"}
def scipy_to_scalar_first(q_xyzw):
    """Convert SciPy's [x, y, z, w] order to [w, x, y, z]."""
    x, y, z, w = q_xyzw
    return np.array([w, x, y, z])

rotation_b_to_n = Rotation.from_euler("z", 90.0, degrees=True)
q_wxyz = scipy_to_scalar_first(rotation_b_to_n.as_quat())   # [0.707, 0, 0, 0.707]

# A body-forward vector points east after a positive 90-degree NED yaw.
rotation_b_to_n.apply([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])                       # [0, 1, 0]
```

. . .

Convert deliberately at every boundary. Normalizing a quaternion controls
numerical drift; it does **not** repair a wrong convention.

::: {.notes}
Quaternions in Software section. The last line is the "known vector" test from
the contract: a quarter turn with an answer you can predict.
:::

## Attitude kinematics

Over $\delta t$ the body turns by $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b\,\delta t$, in body
axes, because that is where the gyros ride:

$$
\dot{\mathbf{C}}_b^n = \mathbf{C}_b^n\,[\boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b]_\times ,
\qquad
\dot{\mathbf{q}}_b^n = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{q}_b^n \otimes \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b \end{bmatrix}
$$

. . .

Constant rate over $\Delta t$ integrates exactly:
$\mathbf{q}_{k+1} = \mathbf{q}_k \otimes \mathbf{q}(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b\Delta t)$.
The rotation vector is the natural attitude increment.

. . .

A gyro measures rotation relative to **inertial** space:

$$
\boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b = \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ib}^b - \mathbf{C}_n^b\,\boldsymbol{\omega}_{in}^n,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\omega}_{in}^n = \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n
$$

A drone over a lab floor can ignore $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{in}^n$. A ship or
aircraft navigating for hours cannot.

::: {.notes}
Attitude Kinematics section. Production strapdown algorithms refine the
constant-rate update when the rate vector changes direction within an interval
(coning; Savage). The INS/GNSS chapter in Part 6 builds the full mechanization
on the second equation.
:::

## Renormalize, but know what it fixes

```{python}
#| include: false
def quat_multiply(q1, q2):
    """Hamilton product of two scalar-first quaternions."""
    w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1
    w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2
    return np.array([
        w1 * w2 - x1 * x2 - y1 * y2 - z1 * z2,
        w1 * x2 + x1 * w2 + y1 * z2 - z1 * y2,
        w1 * y2 - x1 * z2 + y1 * w2 + z1 * x2,
        w1 * z2 + x1 * y2 - y1 * x2 + z1 * w2,
    ])


def quat_exp(rotvec):
    angle = np.linalg.norm(rotvec)
    if angle < 1e-12:
        return np.array([1.0, *(0.5 * rotvec)])
    return np.array([np.cos(angle / 2), *(np.sin(angle / 2) * rotvec / angle)])


def quat_to_dcm(q):
    """Homogeneous quaternion-to-DCM formula; returns |q|^2 * C for a non-unit q."""
    w, x, y, z = q
    return np.array([[w*w + x*x - y*y - z*z, 2*(x*y - w*z), 2*(x*z + w*y)],
                     [2*(x*y + w*z), w*w - x*x + y*y - z*z, 2*(y*z - w*x)],
                     [2*(x*z - w*y), 2*(y*z + w*x), w*w - x*x - y*y + z*z]])


def scalar_first(rotation):
    x, y, z, w = rotation.as_quat()
    return np.array([w, x, y, z])


dt_imu, duration = 1.0 / 200.0, 10.0                         # 200 Hz IMU for 10 s
omega_nb_b = np.deg2rad(90.0) * np.array([0.6, 0.0, 0.8])     # constant 90 deg/s
q0 = scalar_first(Rotation.from_euler("ZYX", [30.0, 5.0, -3.0], degrees=True))
omega_quat = np.array([0.0, *omega_nb_b])
dq_exact = quat_exp(omega_nb_b * dt_imu)
g_n = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 9.80665])
names = ["first order", "first order + renormalize", "exponential"]
q_now = {name: q0.copy() for name in names}
hist = {name: {"norm": [], "att": [], "grav": []} for name in names}
n_imu = round(duration / dt_imu)
t_imu = dt_imu * np.arange(1, n_imu + 1)
R0 = Rotation.from_quat(np.roll(q0, -1))
for k in range(n_imu):
    q = q_now["first order"]
    q_now["first order"] = q + 0.5 * quat_multiply(q, omega_quat) * dt_imu
    q = q_now["first order + renormalize"]
    q = q + 0.5 * quat_multiply(q, omega_quat) * dt_imu
    q_now["first order + renormalize"] = q / np.linalg.norm(q)
    q_now["exponential"] = quat_multiply(q_now["exponential"], dq_exact)
    truth = R0 * Rotation.from_rotvec(omega_nb_b * t_imu[k])
    for name in names:
        q = q_now[name]
        hist[name]["norm"].append(np.linalg.norm(q))
        hist[name]["att"].append(np.degrees(
            (Rotation.from_quat(np.roll(q, -1)).inv() * truth).magnitude()))
        hist[name]["grav"].append(abs(np.linalg.norm(quat_to_dcm(q).T @ g_n) - 9.80665))
```

```{python}
styles = {"first order": ("C3", "-"), "first order + renormalize": ("C0", "--"),
          "exponential": ("C2", "-")}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4.0))
for name in names:
    color, ls = styles[name]
    axes[0].plot(t_imu, hist[name]["norm"], color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=2.5, label=name)
    axes[1].semilogy(t_imu, np.maximum(hist[name]["att"], 1e-13), color=color, linestyle=ls,
                     linewidth=2.5)
    axes[2].plot(t_imu, hist[name]["grav"], color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=2.5)
axes[0].set_title(r"$\|\mathbf{q}\|$")
axes[1].set_title("attitude error [deg]")
axes[2].set_title(r"phantom gravity [m/s$^2$]")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("time [s]")
fig.legend(*axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="upper center", ncol=3,
           bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0))
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.9))
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| output: asis
fo, rn = hist["first order"], hist["first order + renormalize"]
print(f"90°/s for 10 s at 200 Hz. First order: $\\|\\mathbf{{q}}\\| = {fo['norm'][-1]:.4f}$, so "
      f"$\\mathbf{{C}}(\\mathbf{{q}})$ inflates gravity by {fo['grav'][-1]:.2f} m/s². "
      f"Renormalized: no phantom gravity, and the **same** {rn['att'][-1]:.3f}° attitude error.")
```

::: {.notes}
Attitude Kinematics section. A first-order step multiplies the norm by
sqrt(1 + |w|^2 dt^2 / 4) every step. The quaternion-to-DCM formula applied to s q
returns s^2 C, which stretches every vector it touches, gravity included: a
phantom acceleration that wrecks a velocity solution within seconds.
Renormalizing does not remove integration error, because scaling a quaternion
does not change the rotation; accuracy comes from the integrator, and the
exponential update is exact for a constant rate. The same goes for a DCM:
replace it periodically by its nearest rotation, U V^T from its SVD.
:::

## Attitude errors are small rotations

$$
\mathbf{C}_b^n = \exp([\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}]_\times)\,\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n
\approx \left(\mathbf{I} + [\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}]_\times\right)\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n,
\qquad
\mathbf{q}_b^n \approx \delta\mathbf{q} \otimes \hat{\mathbf{q}}_b^n,
\quad
\delta\mathbf{q} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \tfrac12\delta\boldsymbol{\theta} \end{bmatrix}
$$

[Why not estimate the four quaternion components directly?]{.fragment}

::: {.incremental}
- Four numbers, three degrees of freedom: a **singular** $4 \times 4$ covariance
- An additive update pushes $\mathbf{q}$ off the unit sphere
- $\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}$: minimal, unconstrained, near zero; north and east
  are **tilt**
:::

. . .

::: {.key}
Tilt puts gravity on the wrong axes, $\delta\boldsymbol{\theta} \times \hat{\mathbf{f}}^n$:
1 mrad of tilt is about $9.8\ \text{mm/s}^2$ of false horizontal acceleration.
:::

::: {.notes}
Small-Angle Attitude Errors section. A filter that has estimated the error
corrects with C_hat <- exp([dtheta_hat]x) C_hat. That is why error-state filters
carry delta-theta and leave the quaternion in the nominal state (the EKF chapter,
Part 4). The neglected terms are of order |dtheta|^2 / 2; near zero,
linearization is accurate and nothing is singular.
:::

## The Earth-referenced frames

```{python}
#| include: false
WGS84_A = 6378137.0
WGS84_E2 = (1 / 298.257223563) * (2 - 1 / 298.257223563)


def radii(lat):
    """Meridian R_M and prime-vertical R_N radii of curvature [m]."""
    den = 1.0 - WGS84_E2 * np.sin(lat) ** 2
    return WGS84_A * (1.0 - WGS84_E2) / den**1.5, WGS84_A / np.sqrt(den)


def geodetic_to_ecef(lat, lon, h):
    R_N = radii(lat)[1]
    return np.array([(R_N + h) * np.cos(lat) * np.cos(lon),
                     (R_N + h) * np.cos(lat) * np.sin(lon),
                     (R_N * (1.0 - WGS84_E2) + h) * np.sin(lat)])


def C_e_to_n(lat, lon):
    sL, cL, sl, cl = np.sin(lat), np.cos(lat), np.sin(lon), np.cos(lon)
    return np.array([[-sL * cl, -sL * sl, cL], [-sl, cl, 0.0], [-cL * cl, -cL * sl, -sL]])
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- **ECI** $i$ and **ECEF** $e$: Earth-centered; ECEF turns with the Earth at
  $\omega_{ie} = 7.292115 \times 10^{-5}$ rad/s
- **WGS-84**: $a = 6378137.0$ m, $f = 1/298.257223563$
- Latitude $L$ and height $h$ follow the ellipsoid **normal**, not the line to
  the center
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\mathbf{r}^e =
\begin{bmatrix}
(R_N + h)\cos L\cos\lambda \\
(R_N + h)\cos L\sin\lambda \\
\left(R_N(1 - e^2) + h\right)\sin L
\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{python}
a_e, b_e = 1.0, 0.62                                  # flattening exaggerated
t_curve = np.linspace(-0.05, np.pi / 2 + 0.05, 300)
beta_p = np.deg2rad(38.0)
P_pt = np.array([a_e * np.cos(beta_p), b_e * np.sin(beta_p)])
normal = np.array([P_pt[0] / a_e**2, P_pt[1] / b_e**2])
normal /= np.linalg.norm(normal)
lat_geodetic = np.degrees(np.arctan2(normal[1], normal[0]))
foot = P_pt - (P_pt[1] / normal[1]) * normal          # where the normal meets the equator
top = P_pt + 0.32 * normal

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0, 4.1))
ax.plot(a_e * np.cos(t_curve), b_e * np.sin(t_curve), color="C0", linewidth=2.5)
ax.plot([0, 1.25], [0, 0], color="k", linewidth=0.8)
ax.plot([0, 0], [0, 0.85], color="k", linewidth=0.8)
ax.plot([foot[0], top[0]], [foot[1], top[1]], color="C3", linewidth=2.5, label="ellipsoid normal")
ax.plot([0, P_pt[0]], [0, P_pt[1]], "--", color="0.5", linewidth=1.8, label="line to the center")
ax.add_patch(Arc(foot, 0.36, 0.36, theta1=0, theta2=lat_geodetic, color="C3", lw=1.8))
ax.text(foot[0] + 0.21, foot[1] + 0.05, "$L$", color="C3", fontsize=17)
ax.plot(*P_pt, "o", color="k", zorder=4)
ax.plot(*top, "o", color="C3", zorder=4)
mid = 0.5 * (P_pt + top)
ax.text(mid[0] + 0.04, mid[1] - 0.07, "$h$", color="C3", fontsize=17)
ax.text(0.0, -0.1, "center", color="0.4")
ax.text(0.95, -0.1, "equator", color="0.4")
ax.set_xlim(-0.08, 1.3)
ax.set_ylim(-0.16, 0.92)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

[Flattening exaggerated: the real one is 1 part in 298.]{.muted}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Earth-Referenced Frames section. ECI has its origin at Earth's center and axes
fixed relative to distant stars; it falls around the Sun with Earth, which is
close enough to inertial for navigation. ECEF shares the origin and z axis, puts
x through the equator at the prime meridian, and turns at one revolution per
sidereal day (about 15.04 deg/h). e^2 = f (2 - f) and R_N = a / sqrt(1 - e^2
sin^2 L). The inverse has no tidy closed form but a fixed-point iteration on
latitude contracts by roughly e^2 per pass; the chapter has the code, including a
height formula that behaves at the poles.
:::

## A flat local frame has a shelf life

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
NED axes at the vehicle; the rows of $\mathbf{C}_e^n$ are north, east, and down
written in ECEF:

$$
\Delta\mathbf{r}^n = \mathbf{C}_e^n\left(\mathbf{r}^e - \mathbf{r}_0^e\right)
$$

::: {.fragment}
The surface drops below the tangent plane by about $d^2/2R$:
:::

::: {.incremental}
- a millimeter over 100 m
- 8 cm over a kilometer
- 8 m over 10 km
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
lat0, lon0, h0 = np.radians(42.2742), np.radians(-71.8080), 150.0
R_M0, R_N0 = radii(lat0)
r0 = geodetic_to_ecef(lat0, lon0, h0)
C_en0 = C_e_to_n(lat0, lon0)
dist = np.logspace(1, 5, 60)                           # 10 m to 100 km due north
drop = np.array([(C_en0 @ (geodetic_to_ecef(lat0 + d / (R_M0 + h0), lon0, h0) - r0))[2]
                 for d in dist])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.0))
ax.loglog(dist, drop, color="C0", linewidth=2.5)
for d_mark, text in [(100.0, "100 m"), (1_000.0, "1 km"), (10_000.0, "10 km")]:
    y = np.interp(d_mark, dist, drop)
    label = f"{y * 1e3:.1f} mm" if y < 0.01 else (f"{y * 100:.1f} cm" if y < 1 else f"{y:.1f} m")
    ax.plot(d_mark, y, "o", color="C3", ms=8, zorder=4)
    ax.annotate(f"{text}: {label}", (d_mark, y), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(12, -16))
ax.axvspan(10, 100, color="C2", alpha=0.12)
ax.text(12, 3.0, "drone over\na lab floor", color="C2")
ax.axvspan(5_000, 50_000, color="C3", alpha=0.10)
ax.text(5_500, 3e-5, "ship crossing\na bay", color="C3")
ax.set_xlabel("distance due north of WPI [m]")
ax.set_ylabel("drop below the tangent [m]")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The local NED frame section. The curve is computed exactly, with the chapter's
geodetic_to_ecef and C_e^n, for steps due north of WPI at constant height. For
small moves the other way: dN = (R_M + h) dL and dE = (R_N + h) cos L dlambda.
:::

## Earth rate and transport rate

$$
\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n = \begin{bmatrix} \omega_{ie}\cos L & 0 & -\omega_{ie}\sin L \end{bmatrix}^T
\qquad
\|\boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n\| \approx \frac{\text{speed}}{\text{Earth radius}}
$$

```{python}
omega_ie = np.degrees(7.292115e-5) * 3600.0            # deg/h
earth_radius = 6.371e6
rates = [
    ("navigation-grade gyro bias", 0.01, "0.6"),
    ("transport rate: ship at 20 knots", np.degrees(20 * 1852 / 3600 / earth_radius) * 3600, "C0"),
    ("transport rate: airliner at 250 m/s", np.degrees(250 / earth_radius) * 3600, "C0"),
    ("MEMS gyro residual bias (example)", 10.0, "0.6"),
    ("Earth rate, horizontal, at WPI", omega_ie * np.cos(np.radians(42.3)), "C3"),
    ("Earth rate", omega_ie, "C3"),
]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.3))
y_pos = np.arange(len(rates))
ax.barh(y_pos, [r[1] for r in rates], color=[r[2] for r in rates], height=0.65)
for y, (_, value, _) in zip(y_pos, rates):
    ax.text(value * 1.15, y, f"{value:.2g} °/h", va="center")
ax.set_yticks(y_pos, [r[0] for r in rates])
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0.005, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("rate [deg/h]")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

. . .

A gyrocompass senses the horizontal Earth rate to find true north. A phone's gyro
bias is as large as the signal, so phones lean on magnetometers.

::: {.notes}
Earth rate and transport rate section. At WPI (L about 42.3 deg) Earth rate is
about 11.1 deg/h north and 10.1 deg/h up; a gyrocompass works with gyro biases
near 0.01 deg/h. Transport rate is the turning of NED relative to ECEF because
the vehicle moves over a curved surface and north and down keep turning to
follow it. The 10 deg/h MEMS bias is the example used in the probability
chapter.
:::

## The camera looks along $z$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Optical frame: $x$ right in the image, $y$ down, $z$ out of the lens, so a point
in front of the camera has **positive depth**.

::: {.fragment}
Forward-looking camera on an FRD vehicle: the columns of $\mathbf{C}_c^b$ are the
camera axes in body coordinates.

$$
\mathbf{C}_c^b =
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.incremental}
- optical $z$ is body forward
- optical $x$ is body right
- optical $y$ is body down
- Real mounts add a small rotation and a lever arm, found by calibration
- ROS keeps a camera "link" frame (FLU) apart from its "optical" frame
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Camera Frames and Homogeneous Transforms section. The PnP chapter in Part 3
uses this frame for every vision measurement.
:::

## Rotation alone is not a pose

$$
\mathbf{p}^a = \mathbf{C}_b^a\mathbf{p}^b + \mathbf{r}_{ab}^a
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbf{T}_b^a = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{C}_b^a & \mathbf{r}_{ab}^a \\ \mathbf{0}^T & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

. . .

$$
\mathbf{T}_c^a = \mathbf{T}_b^a\mathbf{T}_c^b,
\qquad
(\mathbf{T}_b^a)^{-1} = \mathbf{T}_a^b =
\begin{bmatrix} (\mathbf{C}_b^a)^T & -(\mathbf{C}_b^a)^T\mathbf{r}_{ab}^a \\ \mathbf{0}^T & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.incremental}
- $SE(3)$: the same index rule as rotations, and an inverse with no general
  matrix inverse
- $\mathbf{T}_b^a$ reads two ways: it maps $b$ into $a$, **and** it is the pose
  of $b$ in $a$
- Points get a 1 appended, free vectors a 0. Pushing a velocity through the
  translation is a classic bug
:::

::: {.notes}
Names lie: in the frames chapter's code T_b_w is T_b^w (subscript first, like
C_b_n), while the PnP chapter follows the robotics habit of destination first,
so its T_wc is T_c^w. Trust the docstring, not the name. Camera pose in the
world composes as w <- b <- c: T_c_w = T_b_w @ T_c_b.
:::

## Heading, course, and yaw

```{python}
#| include: false
heading_deg, speed_water = 60.0, 6.0          # where the bow points; speed through the water
set_deg, drift = 330.0, 2.5                   # current: direction it flows toward, speed
v_water = speed_water * np.array([np.sin(np.radians(heading_deg)), np.cos(np.radians(heading_deg))])
v_current = drift * np.array([np.sin(np.radians(set_deg)), np.cos(np.radians(set_deg))])
v_ground = v_water + v_current                 # (east, north)
course_deg = np.degrees(np.arctan2(v_ground[0], v_ground[1])) % 360
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.incremental}
- **Heading**: where the bow points, clockwise from north
- **Course over ground**: where the vehicle goes,
  $\chi = \operatorname{atan2}(v_E, v_N)$
- **Yaw**: the third angle of a stated Euler sequence. In Z-Y-X with NED it
  equals heading at any roll, and any pitch short of $\pm 90^\circ$
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{python}
def ship_outline(heading, length=2.2, beam=0.7):
    pts = np.array([[0.0, 0.6], [0.5, 0.25], [0.5, -0.5], [-0.5, -0.5], [-0.5, 0.25]])
    pts = pts * np.array([beam, length])
    c, s = np.cos(np.radians(heading)), np.sin(np.radians(heading))
    rot = np.array([[c, s], [-s, c]])          # clockwise from north, page east-right/north-up
    return pts @ rot.T


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.3))
hull = ship_outline(heading_deg)
ax.fill(hull[:, 0], hull[:, 1], color="0.8", edgecolor="0.4", zorder=1)
kw = dict(arrowstyle="-|>", lw=2.8, mutation_scale=20)
ax.annotate("", xy=v_water, xytext=(0, 0), arrowprops=dict(color="C0", **kw))
ax.annotate("", xy=v_ground, xytext=v_water, arrowprops=dict(color="C2", **kw))
ax.annotate("", xy=v_ground, xytext=(0, 0), arrowprops=dict(color="C3", **kw))
ax.text(0.5 * v_water[0] + 0.5, 0.5 * v_water[1] - 1.0, f"heading {heading_deg:03.0f}°", color="C0")
ax.text(0.5 * (v_water[0] + v_ground[0]) + 0.35, 0.5 * (v_water[1] + v_ground[1]), "current", color="C2")
ax.text(0.5 * v_ground[0] - 0.4, 0.5 * v_ground[1] + 0.5, f"course\n{course_deg:03.0f}°", color="C3", ha="right")
ax.annotate("N", xy=(-2.6, 6.5), xytext=(-2.6, 4.9), ha="center",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="k", lw=1.5))
ax.set_xlim(-3.2, 7.2)
ax.set_ylim(-1.6, 6.8)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

. . .

A single-antenna GNSS receiver measures **course**, and course is meaningless at
low speed. Initializing yaw from GNSS velocity at the dock is a rite of passage
nobody needs to repeat.

::: {.notes}
Heading, Course, and Yaw section. Heading and course differ whenever the vehicle
does not move the way it points: a ship crabbing through a cross current (set
and drift, to a mariner), an aircraft holding a wind-correction angle, a car
sliding on ice, a quadrotor strafing. In Project 1's Z-X-Y sequence, yaw and
heading differ when the vehicle is both rolled and pitched; in ENU, yaw is
counterclockwise from east.
:::

## Which north? Which height?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**North**

- A compass points to magnetic north: off by the **variation** (about
  $14^\circ$ W in central Massachusetts)
- The ship's own steel adds **deviation**, which changes with heading
- East positive:
  $\psi_{\text{true}} = \psi_{\text{compass}} + \delta_{\text{dev}} + D_{\text{var}}$

[*Can Dead Men Vote Twice At Elections*: compass, deviation, magnetic,
variation, true, add east.]{.fragment}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
**Height**

- Ellipsoidal $h$ is not height above mean sea level
- Geoid undulation $N_g$: $-106$ m to $+85$ m worldwide, about $-28$ m here
- Orthometric $H \approx h - N_g$; NMEA `GGA` reports $H$
- Feed $H$ in as $h$: every fix moves tens of meters **vertically**, and every
  horizontal plot still looks perfect
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Heading, Course, and Yaw (north) and the Ellipsoidal versus orthometric height
section. The World Magnetic Model tabulates variation by position and year; a
deviation card is recorded by "swinging" the ship through a full circle. A
robot's magnetometer has both problems: hard- and soft-iron calibration is its
deviation correction, and the World Magnetic Model supplies the variation. The
mnemonic is from Bowditch.
:::

## Checks before trusting a transform

::: {.incremental}
- Source **and** destination frames in every variable name and docstring
- $\mathbf{C}^T\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{I}$ within floating-point tolerance
- An identity, a known quarter turn, and a round trip through the inverse
- Angle units, quaternion order, and the sign of gravity at every sensor boundary
- Which north (true or magnetic), which height (ellipsoidal or mean sea level)
:::

. . .

::: {.key}
These checks are cheaper than debugging a navigation failure whose plot is only
wrong by one very persuasive sign.
:::

# Linear Algebra Refresher {#linalg}

Every filter in this course is a few matrix operations in a particular order.

[Chapter: Linear Algebra Refresher](https://jbrodovsky.github.io/advanced_navigation/chapters/01-foundations/linear-algebra.html)

## The toolbox

[Which matrix operations does navigation actually need?]{.question}

. . .

::: {.smaller-text}
| Operation | Where it shows up |
|---|---|
| Cross product as a matrix, $[\mathbf{a}]_\times$ | Attitude kinematics, Jacobians |
| $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}^T$ | Covariance propagation |
| Solve, never invert | Gains, least squares |
| Eigendecomposition | The shape of the uncertainty |
| Cholesky, $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^T$ | Correlated noise, sigma points, the PD test |
| SVD | Rank, pseudoinverse, the nearest rotation |
| Matrix exponential, $e^{\mathbf{A}\Delta t}$ | Discretization, Rodrigues |
:::

::: {.notes}
The chapter is a concise refresher that pairs each definition with its NumPy
equivalent; its Quick Reference table is the card to keep open while coding.
:::

## Math counts from 1, code from 0

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Math**: 1-based, inclusive

$v_1$ is the first component;
$\mathbf{v}_{1:3} = (v_1, v_2, v_3)$
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Code**: 0-based, half-open

`v[0]` is the first component;
`v[0:3]` holds indices 0, 1, 2
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.key}
Math $v_i$ is `v[i-1]`; math $\mathbf{v}_{i:j}$ is `v[i-1:j]`.
:::

. . .

A zero-based index is an offset from the start of the array, which is how the
memory is laid out. Blocks follow the same rule: $\mathbf{A}_{1:2,\,2:3}$ is
`A[0:2, 1:3]`.

::: {.notes}
Indexing and slicing section. The book keeps the two conventions strictly apart.
Negative indices count from the end: v[-1] is the last component.
:::

## The cross product as a matrix

$$
\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = [\mathbf{a}]_\times \mathbf{b},
\qquad
[\mathbf{a}]_\times =
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a_3 & a_2 \\ a_3 & 0 & -a_1 \\ -a_2 & a_1 & 0 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
[\mathbf{a}]_\times^T = -[\mathbf{a}]_\times
$$

. . .

Not for speed: `np.cross` is cheaper. For **algebra**: as a matrix, a cross
product composes with other linear maps, factors out, and differentiates.

$$
\frac{\partial (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})}{\partial \mathbf{b}} = [\mathbf{a}]_\times,
\qquad
\frac{\partial (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})}{\partial \mathbf{a}} = -[\mathbf{b}]_\times
$$

. . .

That is what makes $\dot{\mathbf{C}}_b^n = \mathbf{C}_b^n[\boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b]_\times$
and every EKF Jacobian with a rotation in it tractable.

## Rank and observability

Velocity is in the null space of $\mathbf{H} = [1\ \ 0]$. Is it unobservable?

. . .

No: the dynamics carry velocity into future positions. Observability belongs to
$\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ together:
$\mathcal{O} = [\mathbf{H};\ \mathbf{H}\mathbf{F};\ \ldots;\ \mathbf{H}\mathbf{F}^{n-1}]$,
observable iff $\operatorname{rank}\mathcal{O} = n$.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
F_cv = np.array([[1.0, 0.1], [0.0, 1.0]])        # constant velocity, state [p, v]
for name, H_meas in [("position", np.array([[1.0, 0.0]])), ("velocity", np.array([[0.0, 1.0]]))]:
    O = np.vstack([H_meas @ np.linalg.matrix_power(F_cv, k) for k in range(2)])
    print(f"measure {name}: rank(H) = {np.linalg.matrix_rank(H_meas)}, "
          f"rank(O) = {np.linalg.matrix_rank(O)}")
```

. . .

Measure velocity alone and a constant position offset never shows up: the heart
of why dead reckoning drifts.

::: {.notes}
Rank and observability section. The null space of O, not of H, holds the
directions no amount of data can pin down. Part 4 returns to observability with
the Kalman filter.
:::

## Solve, never invert

$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$: `np.linalg.solve(A, b)`, not
`np.linalg.inv(A) @ b`. Faster and more stable.

. . .

Overdetermined: least squares, through the **normal equations**

$$
\min_{\mathbf{x}} \|\mathbf{Ax} - \mathbf{b}\|_2^2
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}
$$

but compute it with `np.linalg.lstsq` (QR or SVD inside), never by forming
$\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.

. . .

Weighted, $\min_{\mathbf{x}} \mathbf{r}^T \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{r}$:
down-weight the noisy measurements. The backbone of sensor fusion.

. . .

Before trusting any of it: $\kappa(\mathbf{A}) = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$. A
large condition number means small changes in $\mathbf{b}$ make large changes in
$\mathbf{x}$.

::: {.notes}
Matrix Inverse, Least Squares, and Norms sections. If the columns are dependent
the problem is unobservable in some direction and the pseudoinverse picks the
minimum-norm solution.
:::

## Two forms of one update

Woodbury, with prior $\mathbf{P}$ ($n \times n$) and measurement noise
$\mathbf{R}$ ($m \times m$):

$$
\underbrace{\left(\mathbf{P}^{-1} + \mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{H}\right)^{-1}}_{\text{information form: } n \times n \text{ inverses}}
=
\underbrace{\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{P}\mathbf{H}^T\left(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{H}^T + \mathbf{R}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{P}}_{\text{covariance form: one } m \times m \text{ inverse}}
$$

::: {.incremental}
- A 3-component GNSS fix on a 15-state INS filter: the right side
- Hundreds of feature measurements on a small state: the left side
- Underneath: block inversion through the **Schur complement**,
  $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{B}$
:::

::: {.notes}
Block Inversion and the Woodbury Identity section. In the Schur complement, C and
D are generic blocks of a partitioned matrix, not a rotation. The information
filter (Part 4) lives on the left side; the Kalman filter on the right.
:::

## Covariance has a shape

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
$\mathbf{P}$ is symmetric: $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^T$,
real eigenvalues, orthonormal eigenvectors.

::: {.incremental}
- Eigenvectors: the **principal axes** of uncertainty
- Eigenvalues: the **variances** along them
- $\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P} = \sum_i \lambda_i = \mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}\|^2]$,
  the total variance
- Use `np.linalg.eigh` for symmetric matrices
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{python}
P_demo = np.array([[3.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
lam, V = np.linalg.eigh(P_demo)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0, 4.1))
e1 = covariance_ellipse(np.zeros(2), P_demo, k=1.0)
ax.plot(e1[0], e1[1], color="C0", linewidth=2.5, label="1-sigma ellipse")
label_spots = [(0.55, -1.75), (-2.45, -1.75)]
for i, color in zip(range(2), ["C1", "C3"]):
    tip = np.sqrt(lam[i]) * V[:, i]
    ax.annotate("", xy=tip, xytext=(0, 0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=2.8, mutation_scale=18))
    ax.text(*label_spots[i], rf"$\sqrt{{\lambda_{i + 1}}} = {np.sqrt(lam[i]):.2f}$", color=color)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 2.5)
ax.set_ylim(-2.1, 2.4)
ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors section; the matrix is the chapter's [[3, 1], [1, 2]].
The arrows are the eigenvectors scaled by the standard deviations along them.
The trace is invariant under cyclic permutations; the classic minimum-variance
derivation of the Kalman gain minimizes the trace of the posterior covariance.
:::

## A covariance that cannot exist

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
Every correlation is in $[-1, 1]$. Is this a valid covariance?

$$
\mathbf{P}_\text{bad} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.9 & 0 \\ 0.9 & 1 & 0.9 \\ 0 & 0.9 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.fragment}
$x_1$ tracks $x_2$, $x_2$ tracks $x_3$, yet $x_1$ and $x_3$ are uncorrelated. No
random vector can do that.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
P_bad = np.array([[1.0, 0.9, 0.0],
                  [0.9, 1.0, 0.9],
                  [0.0, 0.9, 1.0]])
print("eigenvalues:", np.linalg.eigvalsh(P_bad).round(4))
try:
    np.linalg.cholesky(P_bad)    # succeeds iff PD
except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
    print("Cholesky fails: not positive definite")
```
:::
::::

. . .

Filters lose definiteness through round-off and asymmetric updates: symmetrize,
$(\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{P}^T)/2$, and test periodically.

::: {.notes}
Positive definiteness section. Two practical tests: all eigenvalues positive, or
a Cholesky factorization that succeeds, which is cheaper and is what most code
uses. Exercise 4 repairs this matrix.
:::

## Cholesky: the matrix square root

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
$\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^T$, $\mathbf{L}$ lower triangular: half the
cost of LU, and it exists exactly when $\mathbf{P}$ is positive definite.

::: {.incremental}
- Correlated noise: $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ gives
  $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{P})$
- UKF sigma points: $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \pm$ the columns of
  $\sqrt{(n + \lambda)\mathbf{P}}$
- NumPy returns $\mathbf{L}$; SciPy returns $\mathbf{L}^T$ unless `lower=True`
:::
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{python}
P_two = np.array([[4.0, 1.2], [1.2, 2.0]])
L_two = np.linalg.cholesky(P_two)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
z_white = rng.standard_normal((2, 1500))
x_corr = L_two @ z_white
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.2, 3.7), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, pts, cov, title in [(axes[0], z_white, np.eye(2), r"$\mathbf{z}$"),
                            (axes[1], x_corr, P_two, r"$\mathbf{L}\mathbf{z}$")]:
    ax.scatter(pts[0], pts[1], s=4, alpha=0.35, color="0.45")
    for k in (1, 2):
        e = covariance_ellipse(np.zeros(2), cov, k=k)
        ax.plot(e[0], e[1], color="C0", linewidth=2)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
axes[0].set_xlim(-6.5, 6.5)
axes[0].set_ylim(-5.5, 5.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Cholesky decomposition section. P here is the upper-left block of the chapter's
P_good; the ellipses are 1 and 2 sigma. Any square root S with S S^T = P
reproduces the covariance; Cholesky is the cheapest and most stable to compute.
:::

## The matrix exponential

$$
\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\mathbf{A}t}\mathbf{x}(0),
\qquad
e^{\mathbf{A}t} = \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A}t + \frac{(\mathbf{A}t)^2}{2!} + \frac{(\mathbf{A}t)^3}{3!} + \cdots
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Continuous model to filter: $\mathbf{F} = e^{\mathbf{A}\Delta t}$
- Constant velocity: $\mathbf{A}^2 = \mathbf{0}$, so $\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A}\Delta t$ exactly
- Skew-symmetric $[\boldsymbol{\theta}]_\times$: the series sums to a rotation (Rodrigues)
- Process noise: Van Loan's block exponential, in Part 4
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
from scipy.linalg import expm

A_cv = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 0.0]])
print("expm(A dt):\n", expm(A_cv * 0.1))
print("np.exp(A dt), elementwise and wrong:\n",
      np.exp(A_cv * 0.1))
```
:::
::::

## Linear algebra bugs you will meet

::: {.incremental}
- Shapes: $(m \times k)(k \times n)$ only; NumPy 1-D arrays are neither rows nor
  columns
- `inv(A) @ b` where `solve(A, b)` belongs
- $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}$ where $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}^T$ belongs
- `np.exp(A)` where `scipy.linalg.expm(A)` belongs
- An upper Cholesky factor where the code expected a lower one
- Trusting a solution without checking `np.linalg.cond(A)`
:::

::: {.notes}
Common Mistakes section, plus off-by-one indexing from earlier. Every one of
these will show up in somebody's project this semester.
:::

# Probability Theory Refresher {#probability}

Every navigation system is a machine for managing uncertainty.

[Chapter: Probability Theory Refresher](https://jbrodovsky.github.io/advanced_navigation/chapters/01-foundations/probability-theory.html)

## How wrong might we be?

[...and how do we become less wrong when a measurement arrives?]{.question}

. . .

A random variable maps outcomes to numbers: a robot's position, a gyro's
turn-on bias, a lidar range.

::: {.incremental}
- **Discrete-valued**: a PMF with $\sum_x p(x) = 1$ (a die, a grid cell,
  satellites in view)
- **Continuous-valued**: a PDF with $\int p(x)\,dx = 1$; probabilities are
  areas, and a density can exceed one
- Neither is discrete **time**: a Kalman filter's state is continuous-valued,
  evaluated at discrete instants $k$
:::

::: {.notes}
Random Variables section. Discrete-valued states appear when we chop a
continuous space into cells (histogram filters, occupancy maps) or when the
quantity is categorical (which landmark made this measurement). Particle filters
sit in between.
:::

## Mean, median, and mode disagree

```{python}
r_grid = np.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 400)
rayleigh = r_grid * np.exp(-0.5 * r_grid**2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.7, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(r_grid, rayleigh, color="C0", linewidth=2.5)
ax.fill_between(r_grid, rayleigh, color="C0", alpha=0.12)
for value, label, color in [(1.0, r"mode $\sigma$", "C2"),
                            (np.sqrt(2 * np.log(2)), r"median $1.18\sigma$ (CEP)", "C1"),
                            (np.sqrt(np.pi / 2), r"mean $1.25\sigma$", "C3")]:
    ax.axvline(value, color=color, linewidth=2.5, label=label)
ax.set_xlabel(r"horizontal GNSS error / $\sigma$")
ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
ax = axes[1]
ax.bar(np.arange(1, 7), np.full(6, 1 / 6), color="0.7", width=0.6)
ax.axvline(3.5, color="C3", linewidth=2.5, label="expected value 3.5")
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(1, 7))
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.3)
ax.set_xlabel("a fair die")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.incremental}
- Expectation is a center of mass, not the most likely value: nobody rolls a 3.5
- Linear, but $\mathbb{E}[g(X)] \neq g(\mathbb{E}[X])$ unless $g$ is linear.
  That will haunt the EKF.
:::

::: {.notes}
Expectation, Mean, Median, and Mode section. Left: the error magnitude of a GNSS
fix whose north and east errors are independent zero-mean Gaussians with the
same sigma. The median is what receiver data sheets call CEP. For a symmetric,
single-peaked distribution all three coincide, which is why engineers get away
with being sloppy. Mathematicians will give you disapproving looks if you mix up
the expected value (a property of the distribution) and the sample mean.
:::

## Covariance: how errors move together

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbb{E}\left[(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T\right],
\qquad
\rho = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y} \in [-1, 1]
$$

::: {.incremental}
- Independent means uncorrelated. The converse fails, **except** for jointly
  Gaussian variables
- Dead-reckoned position is integrated velocity, so their errors become
  correlated
- That off-diagonal term is the channel through which a position fix later
  corrects velocity
- Shared causes correlate noise (two antennas on one mast see the same
  multipath). Ignore it and the filter is overconfident.
:::

::: {.notes}
Cross-Covariance, Independence, and Correlation section. In a filter the state
covariance is written P; the chapter uses Sigma for distributions in general.
:::

## Bayes' rule

$$
\underbrace{p(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})}_{\text{posterior}}
= \frac{\overbrace{p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})}^{\text{likelihood}}\;\overbrace{p(\mathbf{x})}^{\text{prior}}}{\underbrace{p(\mathbf{z})}_{\text{evidence}}}
$$

::: {.incremental}
- **Prior**: the model-based belief before the measurement
- **Likelihood**: how consistent the measurement is with each candidate state
- **Evidence**: the normalizer,
  $p(\mathbf{z}) = \int p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\,p(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$
:::

. . .

Prediction is the law of total probability, the update is Bayes' rule:
$\;\text{bel}(\mathbf{x}_k) = \eta\, p(\mathbf{z}_k\mid\mathbf{x}_k)\, \overline{\text{bel}}(\mathbf{x}_k)$

::: {.notes}
Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule section. A belief is a probability
distribution over the possible states: picture a histogram with total area one.
The full recursion is the Bayes filter chapter in Part 4.
:::

## Bayes' rule on a 1 mm grid

```{python}
#| include: false
dx_grid = 0.001
x_track = np.arange(0.0, 1.0, dx_grid)


def to_pmf(weights):
    return weights / np.sum(weights)


def predict_grid(belief, motion_mean, motion_std, dx):
    """Shift a gridded belief by the commanded motion and blur it by the motion noise."""
    shifted = np.roll(belief, int(round(motion_mean / dx)))
    half_width = int(np.ceil(5 * motion_std / dx))
    offsets = dx * np.arange(-half_width, half_width + 1)
    kernel = to_pmf(np.exp(-0.5 * (offsets / motion_std) ** 2))
    return np.convolve(shifted, kernel, mode="same")


prior_grid = to_pmf(gaussian_pdf(x_track, 0.30, 0.01) + gaussian_pdf(x_track, 0.60, 0.02))
prediction_grid = predict_grid(prior_grid, 0.05, 0.01, dx_grid)
likelihood_grid = gaussian_pdf(x_track, 0.37, 0.02)
posterior_grid = to_pmf(likelihood_grid * prediction_grid)
grid_curves = {
    "prior: two look-alike markers": (prior_grid, "C0", "-"),
    "predicted: moved 5 cm": (prediction_grid, "C1", "-"),
    "likelihood: z = 0.37 m (scaled)": (to_pmf(likelihood_grid), "C2", "--"),
    "posterior": (posterior_grid, "C3", "-"),
}
grid_ymax = 1.1 * max(c[0].max() for c in grid_curves.values())


def plot_bayes_stage(n_curves):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.2))
    for i, (label, (y, color, ls)) in enumerate(grid_curves.items()):
        if i < n_curves:
            ax.plot(x_track, y, color=color, linestyle=ls, label=label,
                    linewidth=3.2 if label == "posterior" else 2.2)
    ax.set_xlim(0.2, 0.8)
    ax.set_ylim(0, grid_ymax)
    ax.set_xlabel("position along the track [m]")
    ax.set_ylabel("probability per mm")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

::: {.r-stack}
```{python}
plot_bayes_stage(1)
```
::: {.fragment}
```{python}
plot_bayes_stage(2)
```
:::
::: {.fragment}
```{python}
plot_bayes_stage(3)
```
:::
::: {.fragment}
```{python}
plot_bayes_stage(4)
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
The measurement is less precise than the left hypothesis, yet decisive: the right
hypothesis does not shrink, it vanishes.
:::

::: {.notes}
Bayesian Filters in Python section: a robot on a 1 m track saw one of two
identical-looking markers, then moved 0.05 m (sigma 0.01 m); a sensor reports
0.37 m (sigma 0.02 m). Measured in combined prediction-plus-measurement sigmas, z
sits less than one from the left mode and more than nine from the right.
Prediction only moves and broadens; the posterior is narrower than either the
predicted mode or the likelihood. A 1000-cell grid is fine in one dimension; a
15-state inertial error model at the same resolution needs 1000^15 = 10^45
cells. Hence the Gaussian.
:::

## "Rare" is a rate

```{python}
#| output: asis
import math

rows = ["| $k$ | $P(\\lvert X - \\mu \\rvert < k\\sigma)$ | outside once in | at 100 Hz, every |",
        "|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
for k in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    p_inside = math.erf(k / math.sqrt(2.0))
    one_in_n = 1.0 / (1.0 - p_inside)
    rows.append(f"| {k} | {p_inside:.5f} | {one_in_n:,.1f} samples | {one_in_n / 100.0:,.2f} s |")
print("\n".join(rows))
```

. . .

The "rare" three-sigma excursion arrives every few seconds at 100 Hz. A fault
detector that calls each one a sensor failure will spend its life crying wolf.

::: {.notes}
The Univariate Gaussian section: the 68-95-99.7 rule, turned into rates because
sensors sample quickly.
:::

## Multiplying Gaussians is the update

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
Prior times likelihood: **precisions add**,

$$
\frac{1}{\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{\sigma_1^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma_2^2}
$$

::: {.fragment}
and the mean is precision-weighted. With
$K = \sigma_1^2 / (\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu &= \mu_1 + K\,(\mu_2 - \mu_1) \\
\sigma^2 &= (1 - K)\,\sigma_1^2
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Rename: the scalar Kalman update.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="53%"}
```{python}
s_grid = np.linspace(850.0, 1200.0, 2000)
prior_m, prior_s, z_radar, r_s = 1000.0, 50.0, 1060.0, 20.0
gain = prior_s**2 / (prior_s**2 + r_s**2)
post_m, post_s = prior_m + gain * (z_radar - prior_m), np.sqrt((1 - gain) * prior_s**2)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 3.9))
ax.plot(s_grid, gaussian_pdf(s_grid, prior_m, prior_s), linewidth=2.5,
        label=r"dead reckoning $\mathcal{N}(1000, 50^2)$")
ax.plot(s_grid, gaussian_pdf(s_grid, z_radar, r_s), "--", linewidth=2.5,
        label=r"radar fix $\mathcal{N}(1060, 20^2)$")
ax.plot(s_grid, gaussian_pdf(s_grid, post_m, post_s), linewidth=3.2,
        label=rf"posterior $\mathcal{{N}}({post_m:.1f}, {post_s:.1f}^2)$")
ax.set_xlabel("along-track position [m]")
ax.set_ylabel("density [1/m]")
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.034)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=13)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

. . .

The posterior variance never looks at $z_k$: you can size a sensor **before
anyone buys one**.

::: {.notes}
Products of Gaussians section: a coastal vessel's dead-reckoned position fused
with a radar range to a charted headland. Rename the prior x_hat_{k|k-1},
P_{k|k-1} and the measurement z_k, R: the gain K = P_{k|k-1} / (P_{k|k-1} + R),
here 0.86, decides how much of the surprise to believe. The leftover
constant of the product is the evidence p(z). The update is exact only because
both inputs are Gaussian; feed it the two-marker prior and it reports a single
confident answer somewhere in between.
:::

## The one-sigma ellipse trap

```{python}
#| include: false
cov_ne = np.array([[16.0, 9.6], [9.6, 9.0]])          # sigma_N = 4 m, sigma_E = 3 m, rho = 0.8
rng = np.random.default_rng(2024)
samples_ne = rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(2), cov_ne, size=200_000)
d2_ne = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", samples_ne, np.linalg.solve(cov_ne, samples_ne.T).T)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Squared Mahalanobis distance, in standard deviations along each direction:

$$
d^2 = (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})
\sim \chi^2_n
$$

::: {.fragment}
Inside the $k$-sigma ellipse, in 2D: $1 - e^{-k^2/2}$
:::

::: {.incremental}
- $1\sigma$: only **39%**; $\;2\sigma$: 86%; $\;3\sigma$: 99%
- A 95% ellipse needs $k \approx 2.45$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Handed a "one-sigma ellipse"? The vessel is **outside** it more often than
inside.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0, 4.1))
ax.scatter(samples_ne[:5000, 1], samples_ne[:5000, 0], s=3, alpha=0.3, color="0.45")
for k, style in zip((1, 2, 3), ("-", "--", ":")):
    e = covariance_ellipse(np.zeros(2), cov_ne, k=k)
    ax.plot(e[1], e[0], linestyle=style, linewidth=2.5, color="C0",
            label=f"{k}-sigma: {np.mean(d2_ne <= k**2):.0%} of samples")
ax.set_xlabel("east error [m]")
ax.set_ylabel("north error [m]")
ax.set_xlim(-14, 14)
ax.set_ylim(-15, 17)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=13)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The Multivariate Gaussian and Covariance Ellipses section: a horizontal position
error with sigma_N = 4 m, sigma_E = 3 m, and correlation 0.8, plotted as on a
chart. The k-sigma ellipse has semi-axes k sqrt(lambda_i) along the eigenvectors
of Sigma. The probability inside depends on the dimension; the 1D 68-95-99.7
numbers do not carry over. Fractions in the legend come from 200,000 samples.
:::

## Propagation shears the ellipse

$$
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{b},\; \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{A}^T\right)
$$

With $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{F}$ and independent noise $\mathbf{Q}$, that is the
prediction step,
$\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} = \mathbf{F}\mathbf{P}_{k-1|k-1}\mathbf{F}^T + \mathbf{Q}$.

```{python}
#| include: false
F_shear = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]])           # constant velocity, dt = 1 s
shear_means, shear_covs = [np.array([0.0, 1.0])], [np.diag([1.0**2, 0.5**2])]
for _ in range(3):
    shear_means.append(F_shear @ shear_means[-1])
    shear_covs.append(F_shear @ shear_covs[-1] @ F_shear.T)      # Q = 0 to isolate the shear


def plot_shear(n_shown):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.2))
    for step in range(n_shown):
        e = covariance_ellipse(shear_means[step], shear_covs[step], k=1.0)
        ax.plot(e[0], e[1], linewidth=2.8, color=f"C{step}", label=f"t = {step} s")
        ax.plot(*shear_means[step], "+", color="k", ms=12)
    ax.set_xlim(-2.0, 6.0)
    ax.set_ylim(0.3, 1.75)
    ax.set_xlabel("position [m]")
    ax.set_ylabel("velocity [m/s]")
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", ncol=4)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

```

```

```

```

```{python}
#| output: asis
P3 = shear_covs[3]
print(f"Position uncertainty grows, velocity's stays put, and a correlation of "
      f"{P3[0, 1] / np.sqrt(P3[0, 0] * P3[1, 1]):.2f} appears from nothing.")
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Linear Transformations section. Mean and covariance of y hold for any
distribution with finite covariance; the Gaussian property is that y is again
exactly Gaussian. Q = 0 here to isolate the shear; process noise would fatten
every ellipse on top of it. The position error at three seconds is mostly
accumulated velocity error, and that correlation is what the next operation
exploits.
:::

## Conditioning: the update in disguise

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x|y} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_x + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{xy}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{yy}^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_y),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x|y} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{xx} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{xy}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{yy}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{yx}
$$

Marginalizing reads off a block; conditioning leaves a Schur complement.

. . .

For $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{v}$ on the prediction:

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_z = \mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{xz} = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}^T,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{zz} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}^T + \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{S}_k
$$

. . .

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathbf{K}_k = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{S}_k^{-1}
\\
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} + \mathbf{K}_k(\mathbf{z}_k - \mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}),
\qquad
\mathbf{P}_{k|k} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H})\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}
\end{gathered}
$$

. . .

The Kalman filter update. Multiplying densities and conditioning a joint
Gaussian are one operation seen from two sides.

::: {.notes}
Marginals and Conditionals section. The short derivation: the residual
e = x - mu_x - Sigma_xy Sigma_yy^-1 (y - mu_y) is uncorrelated with y, and for
jointly Gaussian variables uncorrelated means independent, so observing y tells
us nothing about e. In information form the difficulty reverses: conditioning is
easy and marginalizing takes work. Part 4 derives the update again from the
minimum mean square error point of view.
:::

## Conditioning is slicing

```{python}
#| include: false
P_t3, x_t3 = shear_covs[3], shear_means[3]
H_pos, R_pos, z_obs = np.array([[1.0, 0.0]]), np.array([[0.5**2]]), np.array([4.5])
S_t3 = H_pos @ P_t3 @ H_pos.T + R_pos
K_t3 = np.linalg.solve(S_t3, H_pos @ P_t3).T
x_post_t3 = x_t3 + K_t3 @ (z_obs - H_pos @ x_t3)
P_post_t3 = P_t3 - K_t3 @ H_pos @ P_t3
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
x_samples = rng.multivariate_normal(x_t3, P_t3, size=500_000)
z_samples = x_samples[:, 0] + rng.normal(0.0, 0.5, size=500_000)
keep = np.abs(z_samples - z_obs[0]) < 0.02
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
At $t = 3$ s, measure **position only**: $z = 4.5$ m, $\sigma = 0.5$ m.

::: {.fragment}
Brute force: draw $(\mathbf{x}, z)$ jointly and keep the samples whose $z$
landed within 2 cm of the measurement.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{python}
#| output: asis
print(f"Velocity std: {np.sqrt(P_t3[1, 1]):.2f} → {np.sqrt(P_post_t3[1, 1]):.2f} m/s "
      f"(the slice of {keep.sum():,} samples: {x_samples[keep, 1].std():.2f}). "
      f"**Velocity was never measured.**")
```
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.1))
ax.scatter(x_samples[:4000, 0], x_samples[:4000, 1], s=3, alpha=0.3, color="0.6",
           label="prior samples")
ax.scatter(x_samples[keep, 0], x_samples[keep, 1], s=3, alpha=0.5, color="C1",
           label=r"samples with $z \approx 4.5$")
e_prior = covariance_ellipse(x_t3, P_t3)
e_post = covariance_ellipse(x_post_t3, P_post_t3)
ax.plot(e_prior[0], e_prior[1], color="C0", linewidth=2.8, label="prior, 1-sigma")
ax.plot(e_post[0], e_post[1], color="C3", linewidth=2.8, label="Kalman posterior")
ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 8.5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 2.2)
ax.set_xlabel("position [m]")
ax.set_ylabel("velocity [m/s]")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=13, markerscale=4)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Continues the constant-velocity example of the propagation slide. The
off-diagonal term Sigma_xz = P H^T carries part of the position correction into
velocity. The brute-force slice and the formula agree.
:::

## One Gaussian, two hypotheses

$$
\text{Var}(X) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[\text{Var}(X \mid Y)\big]}_{\text{spread within each hypothesis}}
+ \underbrace{\text{Var}\big(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]\big)}_{\text{spread between them}}
$$

```{python}
prior_mean = np.sum(x_track * prior_grid)
prior_std = np.sqrt(np.sum((x_track - prior_mean) ** 2 * prior_grid))
near_mean = prior_grid[np.abs(x_track - prior_mean) < 0.05].sum()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.2))
ax.fill_between(x_track, prior_grid / dx_grid, color="C0", alpha=0.35, label="two-marker prior")
ax.plot(x_track, gaussian_pdf(x_track, prior_mean, prior_std), color="C3", linewidth=2.8,
        label=rf"moment-matched $\mathcal{{N}}({prior_mean:.2f}, {prior_std:.3f}^2)$")
ax.axvline(prior_mean, color="k", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5)
ax.annotate(f"mean: P(within 5 cm) ≈ {near_mean:.0e}", (prior_mean, 15),
            xytext=(prior_mean - 0.01, 15), ha="right", va="center")
ax.set_xlim(0.0, 0.9)
ax.set_xlabel("position along the track [m]")
ax.set_ylabel("density [1/m]")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

. . .

Matched moments, peak exactly where the robot is not. Global localization is a
job for particle filters or Gaussian mixtures.

::: {.notes}
Total Probability and Marginalization section, with the two-marker prior of the
grid example. Y labels which marker the robot saw. Within: (0.01^2 + 0.02^2)/2;
between: 0.15^2; total about 0.0228 m^2, a standard deviation of about 15 cm.
The same marginalization, applied to a linear-Gaussian model, is just the
prediction step: read off the lower-right block of the joint.
:::

## Why Gaussians? The central limit theorem

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(12, 3.6))
for ax, n_terms in zip(axes, (1, 2, 4, 12)):
    sums = rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, size=(100_000, n_terms)).sum(axis=1)
    sigma_sum = np.sqrt(n_terms / 12.0)
    grid = np.linspace(-4 * sigma_sum, 4 * sigma_sum, 300)
    ax.hist(sums, bins=60, density=True, color="0.7")
    ax.plot(grid, gaussian_pdf(grid, 0.0, sigma_sum), color="C3", linewidth=2.5)
    ax.set_title(f"sum of {n_terms}")
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_xlabel("LSB")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.incremental}
- A dozen uniform quantization errors already look Gaussian; so do thermal
  noise, vibration, and angle random walk
- Nothing about the **tails**: multipath, rain, and wrong data associations make
  outliers. Gate on Mahalanobis distance.
:::

::: {.notes}
Why Gaussians section. Each panel sums quantization errors uniform on plus or
minus half an LSB, against a Gaussian of the same variance n/12. The theorem
needs finite variance and roughly independent terms. Heavy tails are why the
particle filters of Part 4 exist. The less respectable reason for Gaussians is
closure: when the world is close enough to Gaussian, the math becomes matrix
algebra.
:::

## Never gamble against the house

[Why does the house always win?]{.question}

. . .

An odds quote is a probability in disguise. Decimal odds $d$ return $d$ per unit
staked, stake included, and imply $q = 1/d$.

. . .

Stake 1 at odds $d$ on an outcome with **true** probability $p$:

$$
\mathbb{E}[W] = p(d - 1) + (1-p)(-1) = pd - 1 = \frac{p}{q} - 1
$$

. . .

::: {.key}
You profit in expectation only if $p > q$: the event is genuinely more likely
than the price says. A fair coin at $d = 2.00$: zero. At $d = 1.95$: minus 2.5
cents per dollar.
:::

::: {.notes}
A Case Study in Probability Theory. The same number comes in three formats:
fractional n/m implies p = m/(n + m), so 5/1 is 1/6; American +150 implies
100/250 = 0.4, and -200 implies 200/300 = 0.667. A bet is a discrete random
variable, so this is the expectation slide again, with money. The navigation
theme: a better model is an edge, a wrong model is a slow leak.
:::

## The vig: probabilities that add up past one

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
| Outcome | Decimal | Implied $q$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| Team A | 1.91 | 0.5236 |
| Team B | 1.91 | 0.5236 |
| **Overround** $\Omega$ | | **1.0471** |
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Overround: $\Omega = \sum_i 1/d_i$
- Vig: $v = \Omega - 1 = 4.7\%$
- If the game is a coin flip, a dollar on **either** team expects
  $0.5 \times 1.91 - 1 = -4.5$ cents
:::
:::
::::

. . .

A fair coin quoted at 1.90 on both sides, \$100 on each: whichever way it lands,
the house collects \$100 from the losers, pays \$90 to the winners, and keeps
\$10.

::: {.notes}
The bookmaker does not take the other side of your bet; it takes bets on every
outcome and prices them so the implied probabilities sum to more than one. The
excess is the vigorish, vig, or juice.
:::

## The balanced book

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
Action $A$ on side 1, $B$ on side 2. House profit:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pi_1 &= B - A(d_1 - 1) \\
\Pi_2 &= A - B(d_2 - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.fragment}
Both positive iff $1 - 1/d_2 < A/(A+B) < 1/d_1$, a window that exists exactly
when $\Omega > 1$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Balanced: margin $1 - 1/\Omega = v/(1+v)$, locked in before a ball is kicked
:::
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{python}
d_book = 1.91
f_side = np.linspace(0.38, 0.62, 400)          # fraction of the handle on side 1
pi_1 = 1.0 - f_side * d_book                   # per dollar of handle, if side 1 wins
pi_2 = f_side * d_book - (d_book - 1.0)        # if side 2 wins
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.1))
ax.plot(f_side, 100 * pi_1, color="C0", linewidth=2.8, label="side 1 wins")
ax.plot(f_side, 100 * pi_2, color="C1", linewidth=2.8, label="side 2 wins")
lo, hi = 1.0 - 1.0 / d_book, 1.0 / d_book
ax.axvspan(lo, hi, color="C2", alpha=0.18, label="house wins either way")
ax.axhline(0.0, color="k", linewidth=0.8)
ax.plot(0.5, 100 * (1.0 - 0.5 * d_book), "o", color="C3", ms=9, zorder=4)
ax.annotate(f"balanced: +{100 * (1 - 0.5 * d_book):.1f}¢ per $", (0.5, 100 * (1 - 0.5 * d_book)),
            xytext=(0.52, 12), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="C3"))
ax.set_xlabel("fraction of the money on side 1")
ax.set_ylabel("house profit [¢ per $ bet]")
ax.set_ylim(-20, 20)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=13)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
When the action is proportional to each outcome's implied probability (here,
an even split), the house earns the same whichever side wins. For v = 4.7% the
margin is about 4.5% per dollar, exactly the bettor's expected loss. Only a
balanced book is risk-free: a lopsided book is a bet the house is making, which
is why bookmakers move their lines to attract money to the light side, or lay
off risk with other books, rather than hope.
:::

## Roulette: an edge you can compute

A bet on $n$ of $N$ pockets pays $36/n - 1$ to 1, as if the zeros did not exist:

$$
\mathbb{E}[W] = \frac{n}{N}\left(\frac{36}{n} - 1\right) - \left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right) = \frac{36}{N} - 1
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.fragment}
$n$ cancels. **The zeros are the whole business model.**
:::

::: {.fragment}
By linearity of expectation, no mix of bets and no betting progression changes
it: expected loss = edge × total wagered.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.smaller-text}
```{python}
#| output: asis
from fractions import Fraction


def roulette_ev(numbers_covered, pockets, payout=None):
    payout = Fraction(36, numbers_covered) - 1 if payout is None else payout
    p_win = Fraction(numbers_covered, pockets)
    return p_win * payout - (1 - p_win)


bets = {"Straight up": 1, "Split": 2, "Corner": 4, "Dozen": 12, "Red or black": 18}
rows = ["| Bet | $n$ | European | American |", "|---|---:|---:|---:|"]
for name, n in bets.items():
    rows.append(f"| {name} | {n} | {float(roulette_ev(n, 37)):+.2%} | {float(roulette_ev(n, 38)):+.2%} |")
rows.append(f"| Top line (US) | 5 | | {float(roulette_ev(5, 38, Fraction(6))):+.2%} |")
print("\n".join(rows))
```
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Roulette section. European wheel: 37 pockets, one green zero; American: 38, with
a double zero. Every standard bet loses 1/37 (2.70%) or 2/38 (5.26%) per unit
staked. The American top line (0, 00, 1, 2, 3) pays 6 to 1 instead of 6.2 to 1,
so it is worse still: -3/38. The chapter checks red with a million simulated
spins.
:::

## Drift versus diffusion

```{python}
#| include: false
n_spins = 10_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(36)
winnings = np.cumsum(np.where(rng.random((20, n_spins)) < 18 / 37, 1.0, -1.0), axis=1)
spin_index = np.arange(1, n_spins + 1)
edge = 1 / 37
sigma_bet = np.sqrt(1 - edge**2)                 # std of one +/-1 bet
n_star = (sigma_bet / edge) ** 2


def plot_roulette(show_drift):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.2))
    ax.plot(spin_index, winnings.T, color="0.6", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.axhline(0, color="k", linewidth=0.8)
    if show_drift:
        ax.plot(spin_index, -edge * spin_index, color="C3", linewidth=2.8,
                label="expected winnings, $-n/37$")
        ax.fill_between(spin_index, -edge * spin_index - 2 * sigma_bet * np.sqrt(spin_index),
                        -edge * spin_index + 2 * sigma_bet * np.sqrt(spin_index),
                        color="C3", alpha=0.15, label=r"$\pm 2\sigma$ band")
        ax.axvline(n_star, color="C0", linestyle="--", linewidth=2,
                   label=rf"$n^* \approx {n_star:.0f}$ spins")
        ax.legend(loc="lower left")
    ax.set_xlim(0, n_spins)
    ax.set_ylim(-560, 260)
    ax.set_xlabel("spins, one unit on red each")
    ax.set_ylabel("winnings [units]")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

::: {.r-stack}
```{python}
plot_roulette(False)
```
::: {.fragment}
```{python}
plot_roulette(True)
```
:::
:::

. . .

Mean $-n/37$, spread about $\sqrt{n}$: equal at
$n^* = (\sigma/\varepsilon)^2 \approx 1370$ spins, roughly a long weekend at the
table. After that, the edge owns the outcome.

::: {.notes}
Gambler's Ruin section, left panel of the book's figure: 20 bettors at a
European wheel. Ask the room first: who is ahead after the first few hundred
spins? Plenty of people walk out ahead after an evening and conclude they have a
system. The noise grows like a square root; the drift grows linearly.
:::

## Gambler's ruin

```{python}
#| include: false
def ruin_probability(p_win, start, target):
    if np.isclose(p_win, 0.5):
        return 1.0 - start / target
    r = (1.0 - p_win) / p_win
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - r**start) / (1.0 - r**target)


def simulate_ruin(p_win, start, target, n_gamblers, rng, chunk=1000):
    """Fraction of gamblers who go broke before reaching `target` (unit bets)."""
    bankroll = np.full(n_gamblers, start, dtype=np.int64)
    active = np.ones(n_gamblers, dtype=bool)
    ruined = np.zeros(n_gamblers, dtype=bool)
    while active.any():
        idx = np.flatnonzero(active)
        steps = np.where(rng.random((idx.size, chunk)) < p_win, 1, -1)
        paths = bankroll[idx, None] + np.cumsum(steps, axis=1)
        hit = (paths <= 0) | (paths >= target)
        has_hit = hit.any(axis=1)
        first_hit = hit.argmax(axis=1)
        final = np.where(has_hit, paths[np.arange(idx.size), first_hit], paths[:, -1])
        bankroll[idx] = final
        finished = idx[has_hit]
        ruined[finished] = final[has_hit] <= 0
        active[finished] = False
    return float(ruined.mean())


start_units = 20
games = {"fair coin": 0.5, "European red": 18 / 37, "American red": 18 / 38}
mc_targets = np.array([25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, 150])
rng = np.random.default_rng(1983)
ruin_mc = {name: [simulate_ruin(p, start_units, N, 2000, rng) for N in mc_targets]
           for name, p in games.items()}
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
Start with $k$ units, bet one per spin, stop at $N$ or at zero:

$$
P(\text{ruin}) = 1 - \frac{1 - (q/p)^k}{1 - (q/p)^N}
$$

::: {.fragment}
Try to double 20 units:

```{python}
#| output: asis
for name, p in games.items():
    print(f"- {name}: ruined **{ruin_probability(p, start_units, 2 * start_units):.0%}** of the time")
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Even a fair game ruins you as $N$ grows.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
target_grid = np.arange(start_units + 1, 151)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.1))
for (name, p), color in zip(games.items(), ("C0", "C1", "C3")):
    ax.plot(target_grid, [ruin_probability(p, start_units, N) for N in target_grid],
            color=color, linewidth=2.8, label=name)
    ax.plot(mc_targets, ruin_mc[name], "o", color=color, markersize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("target bankroll [units], from 20")
ax.set_ylabel("probability of ruin")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Here p and q are the probabilities of winning and losing one spin (18/37 and
19/37 for European red). Lines are exact; markers are Monte Carlo with 2000
gamblers per target. The fair-coin formula is 1 - k/N. The solution comes from
conditioning on the first spin and solving the difference equation. Even a fair
game ruins you as the target grows, because your bankroll is finite and the
house's effectively is not; with an edge against you the ruin probability
approaches one exponentially fast. The edge makes it sooner and surer.
:::

## Your gyroscope is a roulette wheel

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Rate noise: angle random walk, $N\sqrt{t}$. The diffusion.
- Uncompensated bias: heading error $bt$. The drift.
- Equal at $t^* = (N/b)^2$
- MEMS, $N = 0.3^\circ/\sqrt{\text{h}}$ and $b = 10^\circ/\text{h}$: **3 s**
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key}
A biased model, like a negative edge, does not need to be large. It just needs
time.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{python}
t_gyro = np.logspace(-1, 2, 300)                # seconds
arw, bias = 0.3, 10.0                           # deg/sqrt(h), deg/h
t_cross = (arw / bias) ** 2 * 3600.0
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.1))
ax.loglog(t_gyro, arw * np.sqrt(t_gyro / 3600.0), color="0.45", linewidth=2.8,
          label=r"random walk, $N\sqrt{t}$")
ax.loglog(t_gyro, bias * t_gyro / 3600.0, color="C3", linewidth=2.8, label="bias, $bt$")
ax.axvline(t_cross, color="C0", linestyle="--", linewidth=2,
           label=rf"$t^* \approx {t_cross:.1f}$ s")
ax.set_xlabel("time since the last heading fix [s]")
ax.set_ylabel("heading error [deg]")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
End of the Gambler's Ruin section: the same drift-versus-diffusion structure as
the roulette table, for a MEMS gyroscope integrated for heading. Past a few
seconds the bias owns the error budget, which is why every inertial filter in
this book carries the gyro bias as a state (the INS error chapter, Part 6).
Exercise 6 does this with different numbers.
:::

## Parimutuel pools: beat the crowd, not the track

All bets go into one pool; the track takes $\tau$ off the top. The crowd's money
implies $q_i = P_i / P$.

$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{profit}] = (1 - \tau)\,\frac{p_i}{q_i} - 1
$$

::: {.incremental}
- The crowd as a whole loses exactly the take; the track never needs to know who
  is right
- You win only where $p_i/q_i > 1/(1-\tau)$: about 1.22 for an 18% take. That
  money comes from the **other bettors**
- Bill Benter, Hong Kong racing from the 1980s: his model **fused with** the
  crowd's odds beat both, by more than the take. That is sensor fusion
:::

::: {.notes}
Horse Racing: Parimutuel Pools section. Parimutuel is French for "mutual stake";
takes are typically 15 to 25 percent. The analysis ignores that a large bet
moves q_i itself, which caps how far an edge scales (Exercise 5d). Two
imperfect, partly independent estimators combined with sensible weights beat
either one, exactly as in the product-of-Gaussians slide. Source: Benter, 1994.
:::

## The only winning move

::: {.incremental}
- Normalization never fails: any likelihood gives a posterior that integrates
  to one
- The **model** fails: a range sensor that reads 2% long gives a confident,
  systematically wrong posterior
- Quoted odds $q_i = 1/d_i$ are a model biased on purpose; taking them at face
  value is running a biased sensor model
- No cheating required: $\Omega > 1$, a take $\tau > 0$, or a green pocket
:::

. . .

::: {.key}
Know your model's biases, estimate them when you can, and when you cannot, do
not bet the vehicle on them.
:::

. . .

"The only winning move is not to play." (*WarGames*, 1983)

::: {.notes}
The Connection to Bayesian Filtering callout and the chapter's upshot. The
evidence p(z) is computed from the model itself, so the posterior always
normalizes. Benter is the exception that proves the rule: he did not beat the
house, he beat the other bettors with a better model while the track collected
its take from everyone.
:::

## Code you can trust

[What separates a filter that works from one that works on your laptop?]{.question}

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- One reproducible environment
- Typed, explicit interfaces
- One shape convention
- Randomness passed in, never global
- Tests that pin down the "almost right"
:::

::: {.notes}
Chapter opening. "Software is eating the world, but hardware gives it teeth":
a career in autonomous systems needs real software skills. The Scientific Python
Library Development Guide and the Scientific Python Lectures are the deeper
references; for coursework, a pyproject.toml and three directories are enough.
:::

## One environment, reproducibly

```bash
# The course repository: build .venv/ from the committed uv.lock
uv sync
uv run pytest

# A project of your own
uv init --lib my_filter        # pyproject.toml and src/my_filter/
uv add numpy scipy matplotlib  # records the dependencies, pins them in uv.lock
uv add --dev pytest            # development-only dependency
```

::: {.incremental}
- Python 3.11 or newer, and **never** the system Python
- Commit `uv.lock`: `uv sync` rebuilds the same environment on any machine
- No activation: `uv run` does it for each command. Fallback: `venv` plus
  `pip freeze`
:::

::: {.notes}
Python Version and Environment section. The course repository is a uv
workspace; every command in the book and the handouts is written with uv run.
Data science folks: pixi manages conda-ecosystem packages and uses uv's
resolver for PyPI.
:::

## Type hints are checked by tools, not Python

```python
def add(x: str, y: str) -> str:
    return x + y  # concatenates two strings

add('abc', '123')  # returns 'abc123'
add(1, 2)          # still returns 3 at runtime, but a type checker flags this line
```

. . .

The interpreter records hints and moves on. `mypy` or `pyright` (inside most
editors) reads them, but only if you run it.

. . .

```python
@dataclass
class FilterState:
    x: np.ndarray  # state estimate, shape (n,)
    P: np.ndarray  # covariance, shape (n, n)
    t: float       # time [s]
```

::: {.notes}
Type Hints and Dataclasses section. Python promotes 1 + 2.0 to a float, as C++
does; Rust refuses to mix integer and floating-point types. Exercise 5 runs both
commands and asks why both outcomes are correct.
:::

## Broadcasting: silent poison

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
z = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])            # measurement, shape (3,)
H = np.eye(3)
x_col = np.array([[0.9], [2.1], [2.8]])  # state stored as a column, shape (3, 1)

y_wrong = z - H @ x_col                  # (3,) - (3, 1) broadcasts to (3, 3)
print("residual shape:", y_wrong.shape)
```

. . .

No exception, no warning: a wrong answer that flows into the gain and the
covariance.

. . .

::: {.key}
Pick one convention, `(n,)` everywhere, and guard it: `assert y.shape == z.shape`
costs nothing and saves an afternoon.
:::

::: {.notes}
Shape Discipline section. NumPy lines up trailing dimensions and stretches any
dimension of length 1: wonderful when you mean it.
:::

## Randomness is an argument

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
np.random.seed(595)
first = np.random.normal(size=3)
np.random.seed(595)
_ = np.random.uniform()                 # a library call you did not know draws numbers
second = np.random.normal(size=3)
print("legacy, same seed, same result?   ", np.allclose(first, second))

run_a = np.random.default_rng(595).normal(size=3)
_ = np.random.default_rng(1).uniform()  # draws from another generator do not interfere
run_b = np.random.default_rng(595).normal(size=3)
print("Generator, same seed, same result?", np.allclose(run_a, run_b))
```

. . .

Pass a `np.random.Generator` to whatever needs noise. For Monte Carlo trials,
independent streams from one seed: `np.random.default_rng(595).spawn(n_trials)`.

::: {.notes}
Reproducible Randomness section. When a filter misbehaves you want to rerun the
exact same noise sequence. The legacy interface keeps one hidden global state
shared by your code and every library you call. NumPy recommends the Generator
API for all new code, and the book uses it everywhere.
:::

my_filter/

## Tests pin down the "almost right"

```{.python code-line-numbers="|3-8|10-11|1-11"}
@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("angle", "expected"),
    [
        (0.0, 0.0),
        (np.pi + 0.1, -np.pi + 0.1),
        (-np.pi - 0.1, np.pi - 0.1),
        (4.0 * np.pi, 0.0),
    ],
)
def test_wrap_angle_maps_into_minus_pi_to_pi(angle: float, expected: float) -> None:
    assert wrap_angle(angle) == pytest.approx(expected, abs=1e-12)
```

. . .

Angle wrapping, frame conversions, and covariance updates are easy to get almost
right. Compare floats with a **tolerance**, never `==`, and run everything with
`uv run pytest`.

::: {.notes}
Testing with pytest section. Test files live in tests/, are named test_*.py,
and use plain assert. Tests that need a dataset you have not downloaded skip
with a reason instead of failing. The chapter also tests that a covariance
update stays symmetric.
:::

## Habits, and the usual mistakes

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Plot routinely**

- Truth against estimate
- Residuals and innovations
- Estimated uncertainty over time

A readable diagnostic plot often catches a model or tuning problem before any
deep debugging.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Avoid**

::: {.incremental}
- Radians and degrees in one pipeline
- Silent broadcasting
- Seeding the global `np.random` state
- Comparing floats with `==`
- Hard-coded constants
- All the logic in notebooks
:::
:::
::::

## Part 2 in one slide

::: {.incremental}
- **Frames:** $\mathbf{v}^a = \mathbf{C}_b^a\mathbf{v}^b$; name both frames, test
  with a known vector
- **Attitude:** quaternions and rotation vectors inside, Euler angles for display,
  errors as small rotations $\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}$
- **Linear algebra:** solve, never invert; eigenvectors are the shape of
  $\mathbf{P}$, Cholesky its square root
- **Gaussians:** propagation is $\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{A}^T$, the
  update is conditioning, and one Gaussian cannot say "here or there"
- **The house:** a small persistent edge, like a biased model, compounds
- **Python:** one environment, one shape convention, explicit generators, tests
  with tolerances
:::
